l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the race is a footrace (between Atalanta and her suitors)
q: I am not,’ says she, ‘to be gained, unless first surpassed in speed. Engage with me in running

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the race has prize Atalanta and Hippomenes' marriage (for the victor)
q: Both a wife and a wedding shall be given as the reward of the swift;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the golden apples is a three golden apples (used to delay Atalanta)
q: Hence, by chance as I was coming, I carried three golden apples, that I had plucked, in my hand;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the golden apples comes from the golden tree (in the Tamasenian field)
q: In the middle of this field a tree flourishes, with yellow foliage, {and} with branches tinkling with yellow gold. Hence, by chance as I was coming, I carried three golden apples, that I had plucked, in my hand;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: wild beasts are dangerous to Adonis (because of their natural weapons and ferocity)
q: Neither thy age, nor thy beauty, nor {other} things which have made an impression on Venus, make any impression on lions and bristly boars, and the eyes and the tempers of wild beasts.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: boars have curving tusks (described as carrying lightning)
q: The fierce boars carry lightning[54] in their curving tusks;

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonis is beautiful most beauteous
q: He, born of his own sister and of his grandfather, who, so lately enclosed in a tree, was so lately born, and but just now a most beauteous infant, is now a youth, now a man, {and} now more beauteous than he {was before}.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: lions is glutted with the slaughter of the herds
q: and the lions glutted with the slaughter of the herds.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the transformed Hippomenes and Atalanta are lions lions (after transformation)
q: instead of words they utter growls; instead of chambers they haunt the woods; and dreadful to others, {as} lions, they champ the bits of Cybele with subdued jaws.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: the transformed Hippomenes and Atalanta draw Cybele's chariot (with subdued jaws)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Cybele has chariot drawn by the transformed Hippomenes and Atalanta (in lion form)
q: they champ the bits of Cybele with subdued jaws.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonis is loved by Venus

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonis hunts wild beasts
q: Thee, too, Adonis, she counsels to fear them, if she can aught avail by advising thee.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus is a Goddess
q: The Goddess, wounded, pushed away her son with her hand.

s: Venus attends Adonis (continually)

s: Venus hunts wild beasts (harmless prey)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus avoids wild beasts (fierce and dangerous kinds)
q: she keeps afar from the fierce boars, and avoids the ravening wolves, and the bears armed with claws, and the lions glutted with the slaughter of the herds.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus is a goddess
q: According to Apollodorus, Venus had caused Myrrha to imbibe her infamous passion, because she had treated the worship of that Goddess with contempt.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Onchestius (city) honors Neptune
q: Onchestius founded a city of that name in Bœotia, in honour of Neptune, who had a temple there; in the time of Pausanias the place was in ruins.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Neptune has temple at Onchestius (city)
q: Onchestius founded a city of that name in Bœotia, in honour of Neptune, who had a temple there; in the time of Pausanias the place was in ruins.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Hippomenes is descended from Neptune (fourth generation, counting Neptune inclusively)

s: Atalanta is a daughter of Schœneus
q: The Atalanta who is mentioned in this story was the daughter of Schœneus, and the granddaughter of Athamas, whose misfortunes obliged him to retire into Bœotia, where he built a little town, which was called after his name, as we learn from Pausanias and Eustathius.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Atalanta is a granddaughter of Athamas
q: The Atalanta who is mentioned in this story was the daughter of Schœneus, and the granddaughter of Athamas, whose misfortunes obliged him to retire into Bœotia, where he built a little town, which was called after his name, as we learn from Pausanias and Eustathius.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Atalanta requires lovers to win the race (the lover has the start)
q: Ovid omits to say that it was one of the conditions of the agreement, that the lover was to have the start in the race.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus causes passion in Myrrha (as punishment for contempt of her worship)
q: According to Apollodorus, Venus had caused Myrrha to imbibe her infamous passion, because she had treated the worship of that Goddess with contempt.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: apples of the Hesperides comes from gardens of the Hesperides (according to some writers)
q: According to some writers, the golden apples were from the gardens of the Hesperides; while, according to others, they were plucked by Venus in the isle of Cyprus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: apples of the Hesperides is plucked by Venus (in the isle of Cyprus, according to some writers)
q: According to some writers, the golden apples were from the gardens of the Hesperides; while, according to others, they were plucked by Venus in the isle of Cyprus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Atalanta is abandoned by father (according to Apollodorus)
q: Apollodorus, however, relates the story in a different manner; he says that the father of Atalanta desiring to have sons, but no daughters, exposed her, on her birth, in a desert, that she might perish.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: she-bear nourishes Atalanta (when she was an infant)
q: A she-bear found the infant, and nourished it, until it was discovered by some hunters.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Atalanta is discovered by hunters (after being nourished by a she-bear)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Atalanta is a hunter (hunting was her favourite pursuit)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Atalanta slays Centaurs (two Centaurs who offered her violence)
q: As the damsel grew up, she made hunting her favourite pursuit, and slew two Centaurs, who offered her violence, with her arrows.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Atalanta accepts marriage condition the race (only a man who could outrun her could marry her)
q: On her parents pressing her to marry, she consented to be the wife of that man only who could outrun her, on condition that those who were conquered by her in the race should be put to death.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Melanion marries Atalanta (after conquering her in the race by stratagem)
q: Several of her suitors having failed in the attempt, one of the name of Melanion, by using a similar stratagem to that attributed by Ovid to Hippomenes, conquered her in the race, and became her husband.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Parthenopæus is present at Theban civil war
q: Atalanta had by Melanion, or, as some authors say, by Mars, a son named Parthenopæus, who was present at the Theban war.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Atalanta is transformed into lion (after profaning the temple of Jupiter with Melanion)
q: Having profaned the temple of Jupiter, they were transformed, Melanion into a lion, and Atalanta into a lioness.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Melanion is transformed into lion (after profaning the temple of Jupiter with Atalanta)
q: Having profaned the temple of Jupiter, they were transformed, Melanion into a lion, and Atalanta into a lioness.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Atalanta is transformed into lioness (after profaning the temple of Jupiter with Melanion)
q: Having profaned the temple of Jupiter, they were transformed, Melanion into a lion, and Atalanta into a lioness.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Atalanta is identified with Calydonian boar chase (according to Apollodorus; disputed by other writers)
q: He also says that she was the same person that was present at the hunt of the Calydonian boar, though other writers represent them to have been different personages.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ælian gives account of Atalanta (a long account differing little from Apollodorus's narrative)
q: Ælian gives a long account of her history, which does not very much differ from the narrative of Apollodorus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonis is a hero
q: and shall the hero, the son of Cinyras, {if} changed, be a cause of displeasure against me?

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus travels with Venus's swans (in a light chariot through the air)
q: Cytherea, borne in her light chariot[64] through the middle of the air, had not yet arrived at Cyprus upon the wings of her swans.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus owns Venus's swans
q: Cytherea, borne in her light chariot[64] through the middle of the air, had not yet arrived at Cyprus upon the wings of her swans.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus mourns Adonis's death (with torn garments, hair, and breast-beating)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus changes Adonis's blood (into a flower)
q: But thy blood shall be changed into a flower.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonis's blood becomes anemone (after being sprinkled with odoriferous nectar)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonis's blood is sprinkled with odoriferous nectar (by Venus)
q: Having thus said, she sprinkles his blood with odoriferous nectar

s: Adonis's death is memorialized by Adonia (annually)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: wild boar kills Adonis (with its tusks during a hunt)
q: Adonis being too ardent in the pursuit of a wild boar, the beast kills him

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonis is a son of Cinyra
q: and shall the hero, the son of Cinyras, {if} changed, be a cause of displeasure against me?

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: wild boar has crooked snout

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV

s: anemone is named after winds (because it opens when the wind blows)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: anemone is short lived short-lived (because winds beat it down)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonia is a festival (in honour of Adonis)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV

q: Astarte caused the city of Byblos and all Syria to mourn for his loss; and, to keep his name and his sad fate in remembrance, established feasts in his honour, to be celebrated each year.

s: Cinyras is a king of Cyprus

q: They say that Mars, jealous of the passion which Venus had for Adonis

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonis is loved by Venus
q: Theocritus, Bion, Hyginus, and Antoninus Liberalis, beside several other authors, relate the history of the loves of Venus and Adonis.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Mars seeks aid from Diana (to avenge his jealousy)
q: Mars, jealous of the passion which Venus had for Adonis, implored the aid of Diana

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Diana sends wild boar (to destroy Adonis at Mars's request)
q: Diana, who, to gratify his revenge, sent the boar that destroyed the youth.

s: Apollo takes form of wild boar (according to some writers)

s: Jupiter refers dispute to Calliope (between Venus and Persephone over Adonis)

q: Venus being dissatisfied with the decision of Calliope, instigated the women of Thrace to kill her son Orpheus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Pliny the Elder describes anemone (as opening only when the wind blows)
q: Pliny the Elder says-- ‘This flower never opens but when the wind is blowing, from which too, it receives its name, as ἄνεμος means the wind.’

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Theocritus describes Adonia (in Adoniazusæ)
q: The festival of Adonis is most amusingly described by Theocritus the Sicilian poet, in his ‘Adoniazusæ.’

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Ezekiel mentions Adonis (as Thammuz)
q: He appears to be the same with the Thammuz, mentioned by the prophet Ezekiel

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonis is killed by wild boar (during a hunt)
q: Adonis being too ardent in the pursuit of a wild boar, the beast kills him

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Osiris is identified with Adonis (by some authors)
q: Some authors have suggested that Adonis was the same with the Egyptian God Osiris

s: Isis is represented by Venus (in mourning for a dead husband)

s: the Sun is personified by Adonis (according to the physical interpretation of the myth)
q: He appears to be the same with the Thammuz, mentioned by the prophet Ezekiel, and to be a Phœnician personification of the sun

s: Adonis is wounded in groin (by the wild boar)

s: Adonis spends time with Venus (one half of his time on earth)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonis spends time in Infernal Regions (one half of his time)
q: Calliope, who directed that Adonis should pass one half of his time with Venus on earth, and the other half in the Infernal Regions.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Adonis is associated with Adonis's return (through an annual festival cycle)
q: after having mourned for several days during his festival, rejoiced as though he had been raised from the dead, at a second festival called ‘The Return.’

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Venus is borne in her light chariot (through the middle of the air)
q: Cytherea, borne in her light chariot[64] through the middle of the air

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Orpheus is a Thracian poet
q: While with songs such as these, the Thracian poet is leading the woods and the natures of savage beasts, and the following rocks

s: Mænades kill Orpheus (in the fury inspired by their rites)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Bacchanals are transformed into trees (the transformed Bacchanals) (as punishment for murdering Orpheus)
q: the Bacchanals who have killed him are transformed into trees.

s: Mount Rhodope is in Thrace

s: river Hebrus carries Orpheus's head (downstream into the sea)
q: Thou, Hebrus, dost receive the head and the lyre; and (wondrous {to relate}!) while it rolls down the midst of the stream, the lyre complains in I know not what kind of mournful strain.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: river Hebrus carries Orpheus's lyre (downstream into the sea)
q: Thou, Hebrus, dost receive the head and the lyre; and (wondrous {to relate}!) while it rolls down the midst of the stream, the lyre complains in I know not what kind of mournful strain.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Orpheus's head is carried to Lesbos (by the river Hebrus)

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Orpheus's head is attacked by serpent (attacking Orpheus's head) (after being cast ashore)
q: Here an infuriated serpent attacks the head thrown up on the foreign sands, and the hair besprinkled with the oozing blood.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: serpent (attacking Orpheus's head) attacks Orpheus's head (on the shores of Lesbos)
q: Here an infuriated serpent attacks the head thrown up on the foreign sands, and the hair besprinkled with the oozing blood.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Orpheus leads the woods and the natures of savage beasts (with songs)
q: While with songs such as these, the Thracian poet is leading the woods and the natures of savage beasts, and the following rocks

s: serpent (attacking Orpheus's head) is transformed into stone (by Apollo)

s: transformation of the serpent into stone transforms serpent (attacking Orpheus's head) (through Apollo's intervention)
q: At last Phœbus comes to its aid, and drives it away as it tries to inflict its sting, and hardens the open jaws of the serpent into stone, and makes solid its gaping mouth just as it is.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: transformation of the serpent into stone produces stone (the serpent's open jaws become solid)
q: At last Phœbus comes to its aid, and drives it away as it tries to inflict its sting, and hardens the open jaws of the serpent into stone, and makes solid its gaping mouth just as it is.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Orpheus's music charms wild beasts (through song and lyre)
q: While with songs such as these, the Thracian poet is leading the woods and the natures of savage beasts, and the following rocks

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Orpheus's music charms rocks (so that they become submissive)
q: The weapon of another is a stone, which, when thrown, is overpowered in the very air by the harmony of his voice and his lyre, and lies before his feet, a suppliant, as it were, for an attempt so daring.

s: Orpheus's music is overpowered by Bacchanalian instruments (during the attack on Orpheus)
q: but the vast clamour, and the Berecynthian pipe[1] with the blown horns, and the tambourines, and the clapping of hands, and Bacchanalian yells, prevented the sound of the lyre from being heard.

s: the murder of Orpheus is punished by fastening down all the Edonian matrons (by Lyæus)
q: Yet Lyæus did not suffer this wickedness to go unpunished; and grieving for the loss of the bard of his sacred rites, he immediately fastened down in the woods, by a twisting root, all the Edonian matrons who had committed this crime.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: transformation of the Bacchanals into trees is inflicted on Bacchanals (as divine punishment)
q: the Bacchanals who have killed him are transformed into trees.

s: Orpheus's descent to the underworld leads to Eurydice (where Orpheus finds and embraces her)
q: His ghost descends under the earth, and he recognizes all the spots which he has formerly seen; and seeking Eurydice through the fields of the blessed, he finds her, and enfolds her in his eager arms.

s: Orpheus is indifferent to Mænades (according to the introductory summary)

s: Orpheus's lyre is carried to Lesbos (by the river Hebrus)
q: Thou, Hebrus, dost receive the head and the lyre; and (wondrous {to relate}!) while it rolls down the midst of the stream, the lyre complains in I know not what kind of mournful strain. s: Orpheus is killed in the murder of Orpheus

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Orpheus is beloved by Eurydice (after death, in the underworld)

s: Orpheus descends to underworld (as a ghost after death)

s: Orpheus finds Eurydice (in the fields of the blessed)
q: His ghost descends under the earth, and he recognizes all the spots which he has formerly seen; and seeking Eurydice through the fields of the blessed, he finds her, and enfolds her in his eager arms.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Mænades participate in Thracian orgies (during their rites)
q: While Orpheus is singing to his lyre on Mount Rhodope, the women of Thrace celebrate their orgies.

s: Bacchus is a god

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Midas's request for the golden touch requests whatever I shall touch with my body (turned into yellow gold)
q: ‘Cause that whatever I shall touch with my body shall be turned into yellow gold.’

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books VIII-XV
s: Midas's golden-touch power turns into gold whatever Midas touches (with his body)
q: Cause that whatever I shall touch with my body shall be turned into yellow gold.
